title: The Behavioral Response of Fish to Flow Velocity Variations During Passage Through a Sluice
content:
ABSTRACT

Over 45,000 hydropower plants worldwide pose significant threats to fish populations, particularly migratory species. This study investigates the swimming behavior of three fish species—Procypris rabaudi, Onychostoma sima, and Acrossocheilus yunnanensis—during passage through a rectangular sluice under varying flow conditions. We employed an integrated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and experimental approach to systematically investigate hydrodynamic-kinematic interactions in fish swimming. By simultaneously resolving velocity fields, velocity gradients, turbulence kinetic energy (TKE), and Reynolds shear stress—and coupling these with kinematic measurements of tail-beat frequency, amplitude, and angular dynamics—the framework enables novel quantification of fluid-behavior interactions. The results reveal significant flow acceleration (0.1–0.6 m/s) and elevated turbulence near the sluice gate, with three species showing distinct vertical stratification in their trajectories. All species preferentially occupied low-shear zones (0.01–0.075 m) to minimize energy expenditure. Tail-beat kinematics exhibited flow-dependent modulation: frequency increased (p < 0.01) while amplitude and angle decreased (p < 0.05), with PCA confirming species-specific patterns (PC1 = 49.9%). Hydraulic conditions significantly influenced spatial distribution, where higher flow velocities (> 0.4 m/s) and baffle heights (> 15 cm) disproportionately affected mid-dwelling species, increasing their spill frequency by 3.2 times compared to other groups. These findings highlight the critical role of hydrodynamic optimization to enhance passage success and promote species survival.
